column1: # The showcase's search index: screen, card id (empty for the screen's header), title, summary.
# Written by SearchIndexTest; rewrite it with -Dgoldberry.golden.update=true.

column4: Every box is placed by flexbox. A row or a column says which way its children go, and the stylesheet says the rest: the gaps, the padding, the alignment and the sizes.
A row lays its children out left to right. The direction is the row's; the gap, the padding and how the children line up are the stylesheet's.
A spacer takes the room nobody else asked for. One pushes a button to the far end; two share the room and centre what is between them.
A masonry deals cards of unequal height into columns, each under whichever column is shortest. This screen is one; the bricks below are a second, with three columns.
A px is a logical pixel, the same distance at any display scale. A percentage is of the parent, em is the element's own font size and rem the root's.
Padding is room inside a box's edge and margin is room outside it, written as CSS writes them. margin: 0 auto centres a box in a container it does not control.
justify-content places children along the main axis and align-items across it. align-self is one child's own answer.
width and height are preferred sizes; min- and max- are the limits a cramped or roomy row cannot pass. Make the window narrower and the note stops at its minimum.
A control's height is a token, so compact density is three custom properties and no rules. Switch it and every control below moves together.
A column lays its children out top to bottom. Nest a row in it for the buttons, and the two describe any arrangement flexbox can.
A stack keeps its first child in flow and draws the rest over it, so a badge on an avatar cannot move or resize it. Alignment or an inset says where the overlay lands.
Two panes and a divider you can drag. The position is a fraction, so it survives a resize; the minimums are pixels. Tab to the divider and use the arrows, or Enter to collapse.
These are the layout properties the engine applies. Any other declaration is dropped and logged, never approximated, and StyleLint lists every dead one in a sheet.
A gap is one length, between rows and columns alike. A row and a column keep their direction; on a panel or a card the stylesheet chooses it.
flex-wrap: wrap lets a row break into lines, and align-content places the lines. Make the window narrower and the chips take more lines.
flex-grow shares out the room left after content and flex-shrink gives it back. flex-basis: 0 with flex-grow: 1 is a fixed share of the row.
An absolute child is placed by its inset from the nearest positioned ancestor, out of flow. overflow: hidden clips whatever does not fit.
A scroll is a viewport onto something larger than itself, moved by the wheel, the keyboard, its bars or Java. An affix pins a child to its edge.
Each header is an affix: it lifts and stays at the top while its section passes under it, then the next one pushes it off. The buttons bring a section into view, moving the least they can.
A scroll clips what it holds and moves it by an offset that survives rebuilds. Wheel over the grid, drag a thumb, or Tab to it and use the arrows, Page Up, Page Down, Home and End.

column3: A log that opens at its end
column4: With anchor=end a scroll opens on its newest line and stays there while you are on it. Scroll up and a new line leaves you alone; load older ones and the line you are reading stays still.
A text is a run of words that wraps where layout puts it, and a link is a word that goes somewhere. Under them are the faces, the paragraphs and the editor every label and field is drawn with.
A text is one run of words that wraps at the width layout gives it. Its rank is a class: display, title, heading, body, body-strong, caption or mono.
A link is a word that does something: it runs an action in the application, or the desktop opens its address, which the arrow after it says. Tab reaches each one and Enter follows it.
Inter in two weights and their italics, and JetBrains Mono, ship inside the toolkit. A weight is any number: upright Inter is variable and draws it, and an italic draws the nearest of its two.
Text scales from 90% to 150% without the boxes around it moving, which every control is built to survive. The factor is applied where a resolved style becomes a font, and nowhere in the cascade.
A label wraps by default. white-space: nowrap keeps it on one line and text-overflow: ellipsis marks the cut; overflow-wrap: anywhere breaks a word too long for the line.

column3: A text that follows a value
column4: A bound text reads its value when it is drawn, and its argument is the fallback until the value answers. Type in the field: the line under it reads the same value.
A face is a typeface parsed once, and a font is one size of it. These four lines are one parse of Inter at four sizes: a second size over a face costs microseconds and no memory.

An application ships a face by listing it in Application.fonts(), and a stylesheet names it with font-family. The bundled families are searched first, and a file that is missing is said at start rather than on the first frame that needs it.
A paragraph is shaped once, and every re-wrap after that is arithmetic over the glyphs. Drag the window's edge: the lines break again without the words being shaped again.

Under every field is an editor: arrows and Ctrl+arrows, Shift to extend, undo and redo, cut, copy and paste. Static text cannot be selected, so copy from the read-only field and paste into the one below it.
A small CSS: four fixed layers, a closed set of selectors and properties, custom properties for everything a theme decides, and transitions that cannot run layout.
Base, theme, application, inline. At equal specificity the later layer wins, so this screen's rule repaints the middle button over the theme's; an id beats a class whatever the layer.

+ and ~ reach the siblings after a box, :has() asks about what is inside it, :is(), :where() and :not() take lists, rules nest with &, and :focus-within lights a box while anything in it has the keyboard. Click into the field.

Flex direction, wrapping, gap, padding, margin, sizes and absolute position compile to Yoga. Narrow the window: the row wraps, each item grows from a 96 px basis, and the badge stays pinned to its corner.
z-index lifts a box over its siblings and order moves it among them; aspect-ratio keeps a shape; a border takes room, and box-sizing says whether width counts it. Both bottom boxes say width: 120px.
white-space, overflow-wrap, word-break, text-overflow, text-align and text-decoration. One line that ends in an ellipsis, one set to the end, one long address cut anywhere, and one struck through.

A colour is hex, a name, rgb() with an alpha, currentcolor or a var(). Opacity on a box with children draws them as one layer, so the left pair does not show through each other; the right pair is two translucent leaves.
background is a comma list of layers over a colour: linear, radial and their repeating forms, each filled in the box's own rounded shape. The stripe marches because background-position animates.

clip-path cuts a box to a circle, an ellipse, a polygon or a rounded inset, filter runs over everything it draws, and mix-blend-mode blends it with what is under it, kept inside its group by isolation.

A canvas asks for frames only while something on it moves. Each tile drops and turns before it lands, a little later per place from the one pressed, then a tile every 1.3 s takes a neighbour's glaze. Press a tile.
An element's first frame transitions from its starting style. A new entry fades in from 8 px above over --gb-motion-base; the ones already there stay put, because an element enters once.
A box with container-type answers @container rules about its own width, so the same children lay out by the room they are given rather than the window's; cqw sizes the title from it.
A custom property inherits, and every colour a control draws comes through a --gb-* token. The second group redefines the accent tokens on itself alone, and every control inside it follows.

A theme is a layer of custom properties; compact density is a handful of tokens that make every control 28 tall instead of 32; always-shown scroll bars reserve a 12 px gutter. Each is a stylesheet swapped at run time.

The renderer scales text between 90% and 150% without scaling the boxes, and every control is built to survive it. It is a switch on a renderer an application builds itself; the launcher does not offer it yet.

Types, classes, ids, descendants and children, a closed set of states, and where a node sits among its siblings. Hover and press the tiles, click into the field, and read the stripes, which are :nth-child(even).
A control with two surfaces is two nodes, and the inner one is a part with a type name: check-indicator, toggle-track, toggle-thumb. The second row restyles only its parts. Tick and switch both rows.

calc(), min(), max() and clamp() mix units when the style is computed, and a length may be in vw, ch or em as well as pixels. Each bar is one declaration; resize the window and the vw and clamp() bars follow it.

direction: rtl starts a row and a line at the right and mirrors the logical properties, punctuation follows the base direction, bidi-override forces every letter one way, and a field's caret and arrows follow its text.

letter-spacing, word-spacing, text-transform and text-shadow change how a line is set; line-clamp keeps the first lines and marks the cut; justify fills each line but the last; and the upright face is variable, so every weight is drawn as written.
hsl(), hwb(), lab(), oklch() and the named colours, color-mix() to blend two in a space you name, and relative colour, which derives a shade from a token: a hover colour with no token of its own.

A border takes room inside the box's width: solid, dashed, dotted, double, groove or ridge, a side at a time, round corners elliptical. An outline sits outside. box-shadow is a list, first on top, and a shadow may be cast inside.
translate, scale and rotate move a box after layout, so a transform costs no layout pass. Hit testing maps the pointer back through the same matrix: press the turned button where it is drawn.

A breath staggered by animation-delay, a turn that never ends, and a plate whose keyframes are theme tokens, so it follows the light. Only opacity, colours, shadows, background-position and transform animate, so a frame never runs layout.
@media asks about the window's size, its orientation, the desktop's light or dark, and reduced motion, and re-runs the cascade when an answer changes. Resize the window and watch the lamps.

cursor rides on the painted box and inherits down whatever is under the pointer. Hover each box to see the desktop's own cursor; grab and grabbing are the showcase's own pictures, since no desktop has either.

Colour, the font properties and the text-flow properties pass down the tree; layout, background, border, opacity and transform do not. The box sets yellow italic and a dashed border, and only the first two reach inside.
A repaint redraws what changed; a restyle throws every resolved style away and reads the sheets again. A theme is a restyle, and Ctrl+T asks for one anywhere in the window. A count is only a repaint.

host.systemTheme() answers light, dark, or nothing where the desktop has no such setting, and a listener hears it change at dusk. The toolkit chooses nothing with the answer: following it is the application's call.

An application's sheet is lenient: a rule asking for something outside the subset is dropped with a warning and the rest is kept. The toolkit's own sheets are strict and refuse. Pick a mode and read the sheet.

The engine takes a fixed list of properties. One it does not know, or a value it cannot read, does nothing and is warned about once. The lint names each such declaration: edit the sheet and read it again.

Size, weight, style, family, alignment and decoration, each a class over one text area. The caret and the selection follow the glyphs wherever the rules put them: change one, then click into a word and type.
What every built-in widget is drawn to: Nord's sixteen colours behind alias tokens, one type scale, a 4 px ramp, three motion durations, and the rules that keep them honest.
Five rules every widget is drawn to. When a screen needs a value no token names, the system grows a token rather than the screen improvising one.
What widgets read: surfaces, text, borders, accent, focus, selection, scrim and the semantic hues. Only these change between the two themes, so switch the light and every swatch here follows.
Seven ranks, each a size and a line height from the theme, at two weights that are two faces: display, title, heading, body, strong body, caption and code.
Lucide on a 24 by 24 grid with a 2 px round stroke, drawn at 16, 20 or 24 and tinted by color like text. An icon-only control carries an accessible name: hover the round button for it.

Every control draws rest, hover, active, focus and disabled, and checked, mixed or invalid where they apply. Hover moves the surface, never the text; disabled is 45% opacity, so a disabled danger button still reads as danger.
Accelerators are written against the desktop's primary modifier, Cmd on macOS and Ctrl elsewhere. A button presses on Space and Enter, a checkbox ticks on Space only, and Tab order is document order.
Overlay by default: a 6 px thumb over the content that widens to 10 on hover, with no gutter. Always-shown bars reserve a 12 px gutter with an 8 px thumb. Switch them and scroll the row sideways.

Built: contrast measured in both themes, every control keyboard-operable, text scale to 150%, reduced motion, 32 px targets, and a role and a name on every focusable widget. Not built: a screen-reader bridge.
A new widget enters with a specification, a metrics row and gallery coverage in both themes before code. The alias tokens, the component contracts and the metrics tables are the stable tier.
Sixteen colours as --nord0 to --nord15: Polar Night, Snow Storm, Frost and Aurora. Widgets never read them directly, and the Aurora hues carry meaning rather than decoration.
Every gap, padding and margin is one of eleven values on a 4 px base, and nothing off it. Padding is 8 or 12, related controls 8 apart, groups 16, the window's margin 16.
Radii of 4, 8, 12 and full. Three elevation tokens whose geometry is fixed and whose alpha follows the theme. Surfaces are opaque, and the veil behind a dialog is the one material besides.
100 ms for state feedback, 160 for a component, 240 for an overlay, on three curves: ease-enter, ease-exit and linear. Exits are faster than enters, and under reduced motion every one is zero.

One focus owner per window. The ring is 2 px of --gb-focus, 2 px outside the control and following its radius, and only keyboard focus draws it. Press Tab to walk it through these; a click does not draw it.
Compact density is a handful of height tokens on :root: controls 28 instead of 32, list rows 26, table headers 30. The 16 px glyph inside a checkbox does not shrink; the margin round it does.
Every control's height, padding and radius is fixed in the base sheet, compact in brackets: a button and a field are 32 (28), a badge 20, a chip 24, a progress track 4.
Three stadium-shaped widgets, one you press, one you read and one you choose, and a fourth with no shape at all that makes anything pressable.
A button runs one action when pressed, and its look is a class: primary, ghost, danger or link. Tab reaches each one and Space or Enter presses it.
A disabled button still lays out and paints, but refuses every route to its action and leaves the Tab order. Turn back and Begin again stay disabled until there is a league to undo.
A chip with a dismiss action draws a ×. It removes nothing itself: it asks, and the list it shows is the application's. Click a ×, or focus a chip and press Delete or Backspace.
A badge is a count or a status that reports and takes nothing back. Its kind is a class, and a one-digit badge is a circle. The accent one is bound to the leagues walked: press a button.
Outlined composes with danger, square drops the radius, and an icon-only button is a circle that needs a name. The + in the window's corner is a button on this card, floated out of it.
A chip is a badge you can press. A filter chip asks an action to flip its value and draws whatever the value says, so any number can be on. A dot is a status, and a disabled chip stops responding.
A pressable makes a row or a picture behave as a button without drawing one: a Tab stop, a click, Space and Enter. It has no words a reader can use, so it must be named. Press the first row.
A tick, a switch, one of several, and one or more from a list. Every control here is controlled: it asks for a change, the application sets the value, and the control follows it.

A checkbox is a tick with a label, in two states or three. Clicking asks for the change and the application sets it. Mixed is a state only the application can put a box in: click it and it asks for all.

column3: A group is one Tab stop
column4: A radio group holds the fact that exactly one option is on. Tab enters it at the selected option and the arrows move and select. A child that is not a radio, such as a caption, stays where it was written.

A select is a closed control and a list that opens in a window of its own. It shows the placeholder until something is chosen, and is as wide as its widest option. Space or Down opens it, Enter chooses.

With autocomplete, the closed control is a field. Typing raises the query, the application answers with new options, and the list narrows. Esc puts the committed value back, and a name no place matches is refused.
A toggle is a switch whose change carries the state asked for, so a drag right on a switch that is on asks for on. This one reads the same value as the Second breakfast checkbox.
A radio is one option in a group: it carries a value and a label, and the group decides whether it is on. These pick the window's light, and the third is disabled.
A segmented bar is a radio group drawn as one bar, with Left and Right as its keys. The bar, the radios, the select and the switch all read one light, so any of them, or Ctrl+T, moves the others.
With multiple, the selection is a set drawn as chips with a × on each. The list stays open while you pick, and change is a toggle: a × and a second click on a chosen row are the same request.

column3: A tree instead of a list
column4: In Java a select can open a tree. Right opens a branch, Left closes it, and only a leaf is an answer. Rhovanion fetches its children the first time it opens.
Two controls whose value is a number, and two that report one back. The slider, the knobs and the first bar read one value, so moving any of them moves the rest.
A slider is a thumb on a track, snapped to its step and clamped to its range. Drag it, or use the arrows, Page Up and Down, Home and End. The class vertical makes it a fader.
A progress bar reports a value out of a maximum, or sweeps when nobody can say how much is left. The first bar reads the slider's value: move it and the bar follows.

column3: A fader in decibels, and commit
column4: scale="db" places a gain linearly in decibels, so half gain sits 90% of the way up. change arrives on every step of a drag, and commit once when it ends: drag, and the second line moves only when you let go.
A knob turns up as you drag up, and Shift makes the drag ten times finer. Detents pull the value to 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100. The large one turns round its dial instead.
A spinner is a ring that turns, for a wait with no measure. Small sits beside a line of text, medium is the default and large stands on its own. Every spinner in a window turns together.
A field owns its caret and tells the model, and a form is found by its fields. Text, a date, a time, a colour and a one-time code.
A field keeps its own text and caret. bind= hands it a value and change= reports each edit, and the field ignores the echo of its own keystroke. Type into either field below: the other follows.
A value wider than its field scrolls under the caret, and a drag is a selection. Click the first field and press End, then Home; drag across the second.
A form finds its fields and gates a submission on them. Enlist asks the form's controller to submit, and every field checks. Leave one empty, or give a port below 1024, and press Enlist.
A row of single-character boxes over one string. Type digits, or paste 123 456 and the space is dropped. Backspace clears the last box and Escape starts again.
A swatch that opens a board: a plane, a hue ramp, a hex field and presets, all writing into the hex. The second picker has an alpha ramp, which is off unless asked for.
A single line of text in a well. This one is bound to the model, which echoes it below, and holds at most 40 characters: a paste past that is clipped, not refused.
A filter rejects a keystroke and never corrects it. A password masks its text and will not copy out, a read-only field takes no edit, and a disabled one is out of the Tab order.
Stacked is the default: each label sits above its control. form.horizontal is a label column beside them instead.
A text field that parses, with a calendar in a popover. Type a date, or press the chevron; nothing before September or after December can be chosen.
The date picker's twin, with wheels in the popover instead of a grid. This one only reaches 06:00 to 22:00.

column3: A label, a control, a message
column4: A field is a label, a control and a message under it, and stays silent until you leave it once. Tab out of the required field while it is empty, or click a label to focus its field.
A text area wraps its text and grows from rows to max-rows, then scrolls. Enter breaks a line, and Up and Down keep the column.
gutter=#true numbers the lines you typed at the positions the wrap put them, so the long paragraph is one number and three lines. Press Enter and the numbers follow.
The containers a window is made of: surfaces, a titled frame, sections that fold, slides, placeholders, a labelled number, tabs and a timeline.
A panel is a flat surface with the theme's border and radius, and no elevation. It is the one container a theme can restyle completely.
A group box frames a cluster of settings under a title. Without a title there is no header and no gap where one would be.
column accordion=#true is an accordion: opening one section shuts the others.
A skeleton stands in for content that is loading, sized from what it replaces so nothing jumps when it arrives. Its shapes are text, title, circle and rect.
A strip of headers over one panel. Close a tab with its ×, open one with +, or drag one along the row. The strip keeps every tab it has shown, so a note typed under one is there when you come back.
A card is a raised surface: a shadow and a stronger edge. With the interactive class it lifts under the pointer. Point at the third one.
A header and a body that folds away. A shut body is unmounted, not hidden. Press a header, or focus one and use Left and Right.
One slide out of a list, with previous, next and a dot per slide. Only the current slide exists. Focus the strip and use the arrows, or press a dot.
A labelled number, with an optional unit and a change under it, green when it went up and red when it went down. The value is text the application formatted.
A statistic can draw a sparkline under its number, the last point marked. The sparkline is given in Java.
An ordered list of entries along an axis. The unfilled marker at the end says the story goes on, Weathertop's dot has its own colour, and Rivendell's marker is a badge.
Three widgets over a model the application owns: they select by id, report what the user chose, and never edit the data. A slot places whatever widget the model holds.
A list builds only the rows its viewport can see, so ten thousand cost a dozen. Click to select, Ctrl+click to add a row, Shift+click for a range; Home and End reach the ends.
A table is a list with columns. Click a header to sort: the table asks and the application sorts. Drag the edge of the Name header to resize it, and Ctrl+click rows to choose several.
A tree checks and selects separately: tick a branch and its children follow. Right and Left open and close, Space ticks. Erebor fetches its children the first time it opens.

column3: A detail pane the model decides
column4: A slot draws whatever widget a bound value holds. Pick one of the Company: the model puts a new widget in the value and the pane on the right redraws as it.
Three widgets that say where you are in a sequence. Each draws an ordered list and a current index; the application moves the index and says which entries are reachable.
A trail of crumbs, built from the model's path. Click a crumb to go back up to it; the last is where you are and does not press. Go deeper until the middle folds into a … menu.
A row of steps: done, current and upcoming, one in error and one passed but not done. In the vertical list, click a step you have reached; the application moves the index.

A wizard puts steps over pages, with Back, Next and Finish under them. The buttons only ask; the application moves the index, and the list above reads the same one. Click a step you have reached to go back to it.
A menu is a widget, and opening one is not: a menu bar opens its own headings, and anything else goes through Menus.open. The same menu value is a context menu or a tray's.

column3: A menu bar of its own
column4: A menu bar is a widget, so a screen may have a second one. Click a heading, then run the pointer along the bar to swap menus. Left and Right walk the headings, Escape closes.
A menu holds items, separators and submenus, and Menus.open puts it under a node by id. Choosing a row runs it and closes the whole stack. Rest on Move to for its submenu.

On macOS a window's menubar becomes the application's menu bar at the top of the screen, after the application menu AppKit provides, and draws nothing in the window. Ctrl in an accelerator reads as Cmd there.
The showcase put an icon in the desktop's tray when it started. Its menu is an ordinary menu the shell draws: Switch the light, Switch the density, Screens and Quit. The first two are these buttons.
A menu opens in a platform window of its own, placed under the button and flipped above it near the bottom of the screen. Press the button, then Up, Down and Enter.
Any widget names its context menu and the application says what the name means. Right-click in the panel, or focus something and press the Menu key or Shift+F10.

column3: Keys that work with the menu shut
column4: A menu bar binds every accelerator its rows name while it is on screen. With no menu open, press Ctrl+Shift+A to add a league and Ctrl+Shift+X to take one back. Primary means Cmd on a Mac and Ctrl elsewhere.
A dialog, a HUD, toasts and a tour float in the window's own layer; a popover and a tooltip open in a window of their own. A message does neither: it is part of the layout and stays.
A dialog covers the window with a veil and keeps the keyboard inside until it is answered. Open it, then try Tab: Enter presses the affirmative button, Escape the dismissive one.
A popover is the panel a popup shows, anchored to a node by id. Press Save: a small panel opens under the button. Press Undo in it, or Escape, or click elsewhere, and it closes.
Message.summary builds one banner with a line per failure, and nothing at all when the list is empty, so a form never draws a box that says nothing.
A banner arrives when the application describes one and goes when it stops. Press a kind to add one, press its × to take it away, and Reset to clear them all.
A tour dims the window except for one widget and puts a card beside it, stop after stop. Right and Left move between stops, Escape skips the rest.
A HUD floats in the window's own overlay layer and reads the frame loop without asking for frames. Switch it on, then resize the window or drag a slider and watch the stages.
A toast is raised through a controller and stacks in a corner. Three show at once and a fourth waits its turn; the pointer on one pauses its timer. Every third carries an action.
A message is a banner in the layout: info, success, warning or danger, each with its own glyph as well as a colour. Dismiss the last one and it goes, because the card stopped describing it.
A tooltip is an attribute any widget takes. Rest the pointer on one of these for half a second, or Tab to it: the tip shows above it and moves quickly between neighbours.
Everything an application may ask of its window is a method on Host. Each card here asks this window and shows what the desktop answered, including no.

Goldberry.launch opens the window hidden, builds the renderer, runs start(host), mounts root() once, then runs the frame loop until the window closes, and stop() after. Everything but root() has a default.

Something opens over a window in one of two places: an overlay inside the window, which is clipped to it, or a popup in a platform window of its own, which the platform may refuse. The next two cards open one of each.

column3: In a window of its own
column4: host.popup opens a real window, measured, placed against its anchor with a flip if it would not fit, and closed by a press elsewhere or Escape. Empty is a normal answer where the platform has no popups.
A desktop integration is compiled in only where the build machine had its headers; elsewhere the call answers that the desktop does not say. Goldberry.capabilities() tells the two apart.
host.badge(n) puts a number on the dock or launcher icon, and 0 takes it away. A Linux dock finds the application by its desktop entry; Windows has no badge, and the answer says so.

A window opens where position() and display() say, clamped onto a display that exists. normalBounds() is what to save: the bounds it returns to from maximized. Wayland places windows itself, and answers empty.
requestAttention asks the desktop to draw the eye to a window that is not in front: the dock icon bounces, the taskbar button flashes, or X11 sets the urgency hint. It says which window, not why.
There is one UI thread. Goldberry.async runs work on a virtual thread and delivers the result on the UI thread, so the callback may touch the window. The window keeps answering while the work runs.
Window.open and Goldberry.run are the whole API for a window with no widgets: paint in logical coordinates with straight ARGB colours, on the platform's own buffer wherever it lends one.
host.fileDialog opens the platform's own open, save and folder dialogs. The click returns at once and the line below fills in when the dialog closes; cancelling is not failing.
host.overlay floats a widget over the content in a corner, taking no space and costing the tree nothing. The handle it returns removes it, at once or the way the widget leaves.
host.systemTheme() is light, dark, or empty where the desktop has no such setting, and onSystemThemeChanged follows it. Switch your desktop's style and watch the count.

host.notify hands a notification to the desktop: GNOME's banner, Notification Center, a Windows toast. It answers whether the desktop took it, and false is an ordinary answer. Click the banner to run its action here.
Fullscreen is a state the platform owns: setFullscreen asks, onFullscreenChanged answers, and the user can change it without the application. The desktop's own control is reported here too.

host.displays() lists the displays connected now: each one's name, bounds, the usable part a window may take, its scale, and which is primary. Remember a display by its name; its id is for this run only.
host.openWindow opens another window with a tree of its own and returns its host. An owned window stays above this one and closes with it; empty means this host cannot open one.
window().close() closes a window, and the loop ends with the last one. onCloseRequest sees the close button first and may refuse it; Goldberry.stop() asks the loop to finish from any thread.
Five dashboard charts drawn on the canvas primitive: a line, grouped bars, a stacked area, a donut and a sparkline. Their colours are the theme's, and each reads from the keyboard.
Every chart takes its colours from the theme by position, hovers a crosshair and reads out the point. These two share one crosshair: point at a day on either and both mark it.

column3: A hole is not a zero
column4: A missing reading is a hole. The default policy leaves a gap, and a lone reading between two holes is a dot. ZERO draws the same numbers diving to the baseline.
An area chart stacks its series into bands that add up to a total. This one is smooth: the curve is monotone, so it cannot swing below zero, and it is applied to both edges of each band.
A sparkline has no axes and no legend: it is the shape of a change, scaled to its own range. It is drawn in the colour it inherits, so inside a statistic it takes the delta's hue.

One line per series, with a legend and a crosshair. Here each series is a series node holding point nodes. Click a legend entry to show that series alone, or Tab to the plot and walk it with the arrows.

column3: A time axis, a limit and a fill
column4: The x of this line is when: the ninth reading is three hours after the eighth, and the axis shows it. The shaded band is a threshold in a semantic colour, and the fill fades from the line toward the axis.
One group of bars per label, side by side and never stacked. The axis always includes zero, because a bar's length is its value. Hover a day to highlight its band.
A donut is three to eight slices, one per series, with a legend that is always shown. Hover a slice, or Tab to the ring and press the arrows, to read its share.

column3: What is not a chart here
column4: No dual y-axis, no colour argument per series, no histogram, heatmap, scatter, pan or zoom. When none of the five fits, the answer is a canvas, a table, or another module.

A canvas is the surface an application draws on itself, and hears the pointer on. An image shows a decoded picture, a QR code is a payload in whole device pixels, and an icon is one outline at the size of its box.
A canvas hands its painter the frame, clipped to its box. This one fills a curve with a fading gradient, strokes it round, and draws a dashed baseline, a dotted ring, a rounded rectangle and an arc.
Drag the plan to move it and roll the wheel to scale it. The drag keeps reporting after it leaves the canvas, and consuming the wheel keeps it from scrolling the page.

An image loads off the frame and is its own size until a stylesheet sizes it. In a box of another shape, fit decides: contain, cover, fill, or none. The first three boxes here are square, and the last is round and clips the picture to its curve.

The icon widget draws a bundled or registered icon at the size of its box, in the box's colour. These are 11, 16 and 24 points by a class each. A name nothing has is an empty box with the class missing, drawn here as a dot.
Image.decode turns bytes into a picture with nothing to close. A frame draws it at its natural size, scaled into a rectangle, cropped to a piece of it, or faded.
Offscreen mounts a tree, lays it out and paints it with no display: a card, two lines and a button, encoded as a PNG and drawn here whole, magnified and faded.

An Input beside the painter makes a canvas hear the pointer, measured from the corner the painter draws at. Move the pointer over the grid: the crosshair lands under it although the canvas has padding.
The editor under text-input works on its own, here on a canvas. Click into the note and type: arrows, Ctrl+arrows, Shift to select, Ctrl+Z and the clipboard all work.
PNG, JPEG, QOI, WebP and GIF decode, and the format comes from the bytes, never the file name. The label under each tile is what the first bytes of its file said.

The same link at error correction L, M and H: the more of a code may be lost, the denser it is. Each module is whole device pixels at every display scale, so a phone camera reads it. Point one at the screen.
An image goes onto the clipboard as a PNG and comes off it in any format that decodes. Click the board, then press Ctrl+C to copy the picture out, or Ctrl+V to paste a screenshot under the pointer.
Lucide's 1870 icons ship as stroked outlines, filed here under 42 categories. The name under each is what icon= takes in a document; press one to see it at five sizes.

The colour emoji face ships as goldberry-emoji. With it on the module path, an emoji in any line of text is routed to the face and drawn in colour from its paint graphs, sharp at any scale. Press one to see it at five sizes.

With goldberry-gpu on the module path a window presents through the GPU, and a canvas3d is a box an application's own renderer draws into. Where there is no GPU, the window presents on the CPU as before.
A continuous canvas3d is drawn on every frame and keeps the window drawing while it is shown. The cube is the showcase's own renderer and shaders; the chip is painted after it, so it is over it.

The UI is painted on the CPU, and goldberry-gpu changes the last step: the frame's damage is uploaded and drawn on the window's swapchain. These readings are that composite, and read dashes where the window presents on the CPU.
Without continuous, a canvas3d is drawn once, then again when its size or its revision changes. Move the slider: each move is a new revision, and between moves nothing is rendered.

column3: What is measured, and what is not yet
column4: Built and measured on Metal; on Linux the composited path has run under X11 on one machine, and Direct3D 12 waits for a host. A device lost mid-render shows black rather than falling back.
A room lit by the hardware ray tracer: shadows, occlusion and reflections traced at the size the canvas draws at, then drawn by the showcase's own shaders. Every setting applies to the next frame.
audio-player is compact controls over a MediaPlayer the application owns: play, the times, a seek bar, mute and volume. The cards drive the same player from Java and show what it reports.
Compact controls over a player: play and pause, the times, a seek bar, mute and volume. Pick a source below, then click the player and try Space, the arrows, M, and < and > for the speed.
open takes a Source of a path or a URI and returns at once. Pick a bundled clip, a live stream, one served over HTTP or a file from disk; the last two samples fail on purpose.
A player reports one immutable PlayerStatus: the state, the position, the decoders, the volume, the speed and what has buffered. It is pushed on each change and read for the position while playing.

An application brings a codec as a DecoderProvider, asked before the built-in decoders. This one decodes 16-bit PCM in Java: play the chime, then switch it off and the same file plays through the built-in PCM decoder. The Status card names the decoder.
The transport bar on its own, for a layout of your own. This one drives the same player as the one above, so pressing play on either moves both.
Every call on a MediaPlayer returns at once, because the engine runs on its own threads. Play, pause, seek, the volume and the speed, from code; the speed moves the pitch with it, as a tape would.
The probe lists every track in a source, playable or not. Pick Two voices, one file and switch between them here or in the player's menu; the position is kept.

goldberry-media reads its containers in Java and decodes with the reference codecs in one native library, with no JNI. The published natives decode royalty-free codecs; this is what this build decodes and demuxes, and which of the system's own decoders are here.
media-player is the picture with its controls laid over it, driving a MediaPlayer the application owns. Pick a source; the cards drive the same player from Java and show what it reports.
The picture with its controls over it; they fade while it plays and come back when the pointer moves. Click the picture to pause, or focus it and try , and . to step a picture and F for fullscreen.
open takes a Source of a path or a URI and returns at once. Pick a bundled clip, one served over HTTP or a file from disk. The H.264 file plays only where the system's own decoders are.
Every call on a MediaPlayer returns at once, because the engine runs on its own threads. Play, pause, seek, the volume and the speed, from code; the speed moves the pitch with it, as a tape would.
The probe lists every track in a source, playable or not. Pick Two angles, two voices and switch here or in the player's menus; a new angle comes in on the picture that covers the position.
Decoding uses the GPU's video engine where there is one, and hands over to software when it cannot. Switching reopens the source where it was; the decoder line says which one plays.

goldberry-media reads its containers in Java and decodes with the reference codecs in one native library, with no JNI. The published natives decode royalty-free codecs; this is what this build decodes and demuxes, and which of the system's own decoders are here.
A player's pictures and nothing else, for an application that draws its own controls. This one shows the player above, filling its box, with a media-controls bar under it.
A player reports one immutable PlayerStatus: the state, the position, the decoders, the volume, the speed and what has buffered. It is pushed on each change and read for the position while playing.
Text subtitles are read in Java from a SubRip, WebVTT, ASS or MP4 text track, or from a SubRip or WebVTT file. Pick the subtitled clip, then show a track or load a file over it.

A Markdown document drawn as ordinary widgets under the theme. Type on the left and the right follows, because both sides are one property. Press a link or tick a box, and drag across the text to select it.

An HTML page parsed in Java and drawn with the same widgets as Markdown, so it follows the theme. Type on the left and the page follows. Press a link, and the line above the page says what the application was handed.

A real web page in the window, drawn by the desktop's own engine over the widget's box. Type an address and press Go, load the page that calls into Java, or open a dialog and watch the page stand aside for it.
Pointer, wheel and keyboard events go through one router that remembers who is hovered, pressed and focused. Each pad here reports what it is told.
A press goes down through every ancestor (capture), reaches the deepest box (target), then climbs back up (bubble). consume() stops it at any step.
A press keeps the pointer until the release, so a drag that leaves a widget still reaches it. Press in the pad, drag well outside it and let go: it reports every move.

column3: Keys and text are different events
column4: A key event is a key going down or up; a text event is what the keyboard or the input method committed. Click the pad and type: Shift+A is two keys and one letter, and a dead key is a key with no text.

One widget has the keyboard. A press or Tab moves it, and host.focus(id) moves it from Java, refused for a node that is disabled or behind a modal. A ring is drawn only when focus came from the keyboard.
The cursor is a property of the painted box, set from CSS or from code, and it covers everything drawn inside the box. Move the pointer across the boxes.

grab and grabbing have no system cursor anywhere, so the showcase draws its own hands at four sizes and gives them to Application.cursors(). Pick the card up: the hand closes mid-drag, because the box holding the pointer changed its own cursor.

A widget takes part in input by implementing Handles, where every method has a default: pointer and key handlers in two phases, text, focus, the Tab scope and the caret. A canvas takes the same through its own Input.
Moved, pressed, released, entered, exited, clicked and wheel. A click is a press and its release on the same node: press here, drag off and let go, and no click arrives.
The router remembers a gesture for the widget: pressX and pressY are where the button went down, dragX and dragY how far it has moved since, and fractionX where the pointer is along the box, 0 to 1.
A wheel event is in lines, fractional and positive down: deltaY keeps a touchpad's fractions and ticksY counts a mouse's detents. Roll over the plan to zoom it, and drag to move it.
An accelerator belongs to the window and fires only after the focused widget declined the key, so a field keeps its own Ctrl+A. Press Ctrl+J anywhere, even in the field.

column3: A composite is one Tab stop
column4: A radio group, a tab list or a toolbar is one Tab stop, and the arrows move inside it; Tab enters at the checked one. Tab into the group, use the arrows, then Tab on: the three buttons are three stops.
A drop arrives as one event with every path and the point it landed on, so a board knows where to put it. Drag files or text from another application onto this window.
context-menu="name" on any widget names a menu. A right-click, the Menu key or Shift+F10 finds the name by walking up from where it happened, and the application says what the name opens.
Where a slow start or a slow frame went, what the platform's libraries said, which way this window presents and what this build can do.

Goldberry logs through SLF4J and binds no provider. Add one and level the toolkit under dev.goldberry: DEBUG is the window's lifecycle, TRACE adds the start-up timeline and a line per frame. Here is what this run lets through.
At TRACE every painted frame logs its stage timings. A hud draws the same numbers live; it never asks for a frame, so move the pointer or press the button to see it update.

The desktop integrations are compiled in only where the build machine had the headers. Goldberry.capabilities() answers from the library's own record, before any window opens. This is the answer for this build.
The messages that come up most, what each means and where to read more: a misspelt action or binding, an expression in bind=, an unknown node, a missing native library.
At TRACE the toolkit prints a table after the first frame, each phase measured from process start. Startup.mark adds rows of your own; this is what Startup.sinceProcessStart() said for this window.
GLib and SDL log as ordinary SLF4J events on native.<library>.<subsystem>, so each is levelled or switched off by name. -Dgoldberry.log.native=false gives them stderr back.
Each window logs one line when it starts presenting a different way, through the GPU or on the CPU, with the reason. window.presentation() is the same fact; this badge reads it.
Each is read from -Dname=value on the command line, or set before the toolkit starts. The value beside each is what this run was given.
How an application is put together: values, actions, views and the one class that owns the window, and the markup the views are written in.
Values are a @Model class of fields, actions an @Actions record, views are widgets or a document, and one Application owns the window. Data flows down, events flow up.
An action is a method on an @Actions record, named by press=. These buttons call app.click, app.undo and app.reset, which assign app.clicks; the badge reads it and redraws.

column3: What a view may not do
column4: Write. A bound widget is handed a value with no set on it, so a control reports what the user did as an action and the model decides. Who changed this always has an answer.
One class implements Application and is the only one that knows a window exists. Its models() list is the whole of the wiring: what markup resolves against, and what repaints and restyles.
Annotate a widget record with @Markup and give it a static inflate method. The build collects the module's widgets into a catalogue, so any application with the module on its path can name the node.

A value a widget shows is a @Bind field; what a button does is an @Action; a caret is widget State; an icon is opened in start and closed in stop; a menu belongs to the Application, which has the Host.
What a user waits for is the process. A native image puts a window up fastest; on the JVM, an AOT cache trained on your own screens loads and links the classes ahead of time.
Your model is plain Java. One Gradle plugin or Maven execution rewrites assignments to its fields so they notify, and forgetting it is a loud error naming the step.
A document names what it cannot build. press= and change= name actions, bind= names a value, icon= names an icon built once, and controller= names an object. Each resolves in a registry of its own.
ReloadableSource keeps the last version of a file that parsed and HotReload watches it. A broken save leaves the last good document in force and logs the failure; the next save gets another go.
A document inflates to an ordinary widget, so it goes wherever a widget goes. The first button here is markup, the second is Java, and both press app.click.
A value is a @Bind field on a @Model class. A slider, a knob, a bar and a line of text all read app.gain here: drag one and the rest follow, because there is one value and four readers.
A view is a widget record or a document, and both name a value the same way: bind="app.clicks" and Models.observable(model, "app.clicks") are one lookup.
A caret, a scroll offset or a hover is the widget's and dies with it. A value a second screen would need to agree on is the application's. Count with both buttons.

Actions that need the window, such as showing the frame readout, live on a record of their own beside the view model. One document presses both: the first button is the window's, the second the model's.
Views in a package of their own, so they can be replaced without touching the model. Everything else is flat.
KdlParser turns text into nodes that carry their line and column, and KdlInflater turns nodes into widgets. Widget names need no registration: every widget module on the path announces its own.
Any node takes id=, class=, tooltip=, context-menu=, name= and, on a control, disabled=. Hover the first button for its tooltip, right-click it for a menu, and Tab past the one that is disabled.
A document has no loop and no conditional. One mark per league walked is a row whose length follows a value, so it is built in Java.
Widgets.inflater(icons, models) turns parsed nodes into widgets resolved against your models. Edit the document: it is parsed and inflated again on every keystroke.
KDL 2.0: a node is a name, arguments, properties and a child block. Keywords are #true and #false, /- comments out a node. Try a bare true and see it refused.
A name nothing registered fails at inflation, with the bound names listed, because a button that silently does nothing is the hardest bug to notice. Fix the typo to app.click.
A binding is a name or names joined by dots, never an expression. Negation, formatting and arithmetic stay in Java. Take the ! out and the text follows app.light.
A music streaming app made of the stock rows, pressables, icons and sliders and dressed by one stylesheet. Open a playlist, play a track, like it, shuffle, seek and open the now-playing panel.
